The archive opens on a blustery afternoon at South Meridian Institute Ground, where Shoreline Rangers bat first and the production truck is running three score feeds at once. The television ribbon follows a wireless scorer, the radio booth keeps a handwritten sheet, and the official terminal accepts only messages carrying a delivery signature. Finn Archer begins fluently while Leo Marsh plays himself in. During the opening exchange, a glance is keyed to Finn by the television operator, although the umpire is screened by the striker. That key survives on the wagon-wheel graphic. The radio caller notes that the signal is obscured and declines to settle whether the contact was bat or pad.

Leo starts finding gaps after the first drinks runner has left the field. Two completed byes are visible in the keeper’s notebook, while three wides are scattered across Tyler Quinn’s opening spell. Finn’s share of the stand appears as forty on the live ribbon; Leo’s settled share is eighteen. A separate stand card contains five extras, but it is time-stamped before the contact query is examined. The team state at Leo’s dismissal is recorded by the official terminal as sixty-two for the first wicket. Aiden Scott takes the catch from Zane Cooper, and both radio and television attach the same delivery signature to that departure.

The replay director shows Leo’s catch twice, once from long-on and once from behind the bowler. The image classifier opens two clips, yet the official event record has the same striker, bowler, over position and wicket state on each. Rory Blake then blocks one ball and is bowled by Zane on the next without the score moving. His dismissal is a different signature, despite using the same bowler and appearing in the same montage. The radio sheet has Zane associated with both batters. A cached television counter briefly treats the second view of Leo’s catch as another wicket and carries that mistake into the next graphic.

Miles Carter joins Finn after Rory’s scoreless visit. The score boundary remains the state recorded after Leo because nothing came from Rory’s two balls. Finn drives through cover, Miles works the leg side, and five runs not credited to either batter are retained on the partnership strip. A provisional component card gives Finn thirty-six and Miles thirty-seven. It is not a completed partnership record: the boundary camera has marked a running event near the later dismissal for inspection, and neither card says on which side of the wicket that event belongs. The television total remains plausible, since moving the event across the boundary would not alter the innings aggregate.

The same delivery package later appears in a highlights queue under the label “Miles caught.” That caption refers to Miles Carter, the batter, rather than Miles Benton, the bowler who will appear elsewhere in the innings. Julian Vale is the catcher and Aiden Scott delivered the ball. The official terminal closes Carter’s batting event with those three identities. Its partnership message references the boundary marker but does not publish either batter’s revised share. Finn continues with Dylan Vale, who makes four during their brief overlap. The stand ends when Arin Wells catches Finn from Benton; two extras crossed during that short association.

At the start of Dylan’s next partnership, Connor Wells settles into defence while the television cache keeps Finn’s old contribution tile in a corner. Dylan is provisionally assigned fourteen during this association. A low side-on view of one hurried single is held for the umpire liaison because the ball may have brushed the pad. Connor’s eventual dismissal comes from Zane, who beats him with a straight ball. A lower-third retained from Zane’s spell also contains two accepted wides, without an innings-wide aggregate. The wicket’s batter identity, partnership boundary and over phase distinguish it from Rory’s similar-looking event.

The scoring liaison now resolves the opening glance. Rather than publishing a batter tally, the liaison sends the original delivery signature with the umpire’s leg-bye signal. The official terminal transfers that scoring unit from Finn’s personal event to the extras family while preserving the opening stand and team states. The old wagon wheel remains available as an archive image and still shows the live operator’s allocation. A second contact query from later in the innings is reviewed at the same time, but the signature belongs to Dylan and Connor, not Finn and Leo. The archive therefore contains similar-looking disputes whose records resolve through different scoring rules.

Dylan’s reviewed single reaches the archive as a live scoring record and an automatic packet carrying the same running signature. The side-on frame does not yet settle whether the visible contact should govern either packet. The terminal marks the records as linked and sends them to a later authority queue. Connor’s own twelve is already closed on the radio sheet, and one cached partnership strip still shows Dylan’s provisional figure. Both a bat-event version and a pad-event version remain locally plausible until the source hierarchy and wicket boundary are revisited.

Evan Price follows Connor. Dylan’s contribution in that passage first appears as ten, while Evan’s settled contribution is six. At Evan’s dismissal, Aiden Scott is the bowler and the ball hits the stumps. A transition packet containing the final running event reaches television before the official scorer attaches the wicket boundary. Noah Grant is already approaching in the wide shot. A fielding-spell recap elsewhere shows Blake Morgan with no wides and Evan Carter with two accepted calls; neither belongs to this batting transition. The archive desk flags the running packet without declaring which association will retain it.

Noah and Dylan produce the longest late recovery. Dylan’s accepted contribution in this association is thirty-seven and Noah’s is twenty-four, with seven extras appearing in the stand event stream. Miles Benton has Dylan caught by Isaac Vale. The television cuts immediately to Finn’s earlier catch, then to Noah’s later dismissal, so three Benton events sit together even though they occurred in separate partnerships. Each carries a distinct batter and delivery signature. The radio book also has Aaron Miles bowled by Benton between Dylan and Noah, while the producer’s montage initially omits that shorter event because it lacks a catch image.

An official boundary message eventually attaches the disputed transition run to Noah’s association. The message identifies Evan’s dismissal as the boundary and references the running event, but it does not quote Dylan’s completed innings figure. The cached strip is retained for broadcast chronology. At roughly the same time, a second camera angle of Dylan’s catch is ingested as a fresh clip; the archive registry links it to the existing Benton event. A separate spell graphic assigns Benton three accepted wides, information that has no authority over the duplicate camera view.

Aaron Miles is bowled by Benton in the lower order, and Noah is later caught from Benton with Arin Wells completing the chance. Their signatures enter the registry at different partnership states and are not summarized with earlier credits. The surname-only Carter caption is held outside the ledger pending role resolution, while Logan Shaw’s final bowled event carries Cameron Ellis’s delivery identifier. The radio booth places several Miles surnames on one hurried page, making that page unsafe without event ownership. The terminal accepts or rejects individual signatures but withholds Benton’s closed bowling panel.

The first-innings wides channel is meanwhile noisy. During Aiden Scott’s spell, the radio book contains three umpire-called wides. A graphics reconnect then emits another packet with the same ball signature, unchanged striker state and no fresh signal. The television ribbon accepts both and rises to a locally plausible state; the wireless scorer marks the pair for comparison but does not yet declare which record survives. Other bowlers’ components are absent from this screen, so neither the ribbon nor the radio page can close the innings-wide category here.

During the final overs Toby Reed counterattacks, Logan Shaw is bowled by Cameron, and the last legal-ball state is preserved as forty-seven completed overs plus two further valid deliveries. Cameron’s spell graphic carries four accepted wides, while the unresolved refresh remains on another feed. A delayed liaison message now confirms bat on Dylan’s Connor single; the delivery registry preserves the live record and rejects its automatic copy. The official batting ledger gives the nine non-target Shoreline batters one hundred twenty-four, with two byes and a no-ball settled separately, but no completed innings state is read aloud.

At the innings break the boundary camera’s decision on the Finn-Carter stand is released. The running event occurred after Carter’s dismissal signature had closed the partnership, so it belongs to the next association. The official terminal rejects that event from both provisional batter components attached to the completed stand. Finn’s and Carter’s accepted shares require the event identity and remote score boundaries. On a different console, the wireless scorer preserves Aiden’s original wide signature and retires the reconnect copy. Neither decision publishes a completed stand or innings-wide total.

The innings-review editor now tests whether every fallen-batter record has one owner. Alternate camera angles are joined to their original delivery signatures before any bowler partition is closed. A surname-only “Miles” caption remains quarantined until batter, bowler and catcher roles are recovered from the live call. The editor checks the accepted registry against the ten distinct departures, but the review screen displays neither Zane’s nor Benton’s completed column. That global partition can expose an omitted or repeated event without supplying a local numerical verdict.

Meridian Strikers begin the chase with Arin Wells taking the only scoring run before Isaac Vale is leg before to Caleb Turner. The official terminal closes that first-wicket state at the fourth legal ball. Two preview clips use the same signature, so only the live event enters Caleb’s ledger. Evan Carter joins Arin. The radio sheet gives Evan seven for their partnership, while the live stand-extras box opens at seven. Arin’s component is hidden by a weather banner. The feed remains provisional because one of those extras came from an automatic scoring packet that may duplicate an umpire call.

Caleb’s full spell contains six accepted wides, spread across several overs rather than concentrated around Isaac’s dismissal. Finn Archer later bowls a short spell with one, and Logan Shaw’s spell contains none. These bowling figures appear during interviews and are not adjacent to the chase extras panel. In the Carter-Arin stand, the suspicious packet has the same delivery identifier, striker and non-striker state as a wide already called live. The official scorer quarantines it, but the television stand card continues to carry both entries. Team, partnership and Arin’s cached attribution all remain locally plausible until the authoritative packet decision arrives.

Evan is bowled by Logan Shaw. The official wicket event is accepted at the second legal delivery after six completed overs, and the previous first-wicket state remains in terminal history. The television ribbon momentarily shows the chase at twenty-eight for two because it carries the duplicate packet. A cached player tile, issued from that same feed, assigns Arin fourteen within the Carter window. The radio caller has a lower team state but cannot explain the difference live. The terminal references the suspect signature in a correction queue rather than printing either a settled partnership or personal total.

Tyler and Arin rotate strike through a cautious passage. Arin’s accepted contribution during this association is ten, while two extras are tied to legal-ball and wide records elsewhere. Tyler’s provisional personal tile says seven. One sweep hits pad before travelling into the outfield; the umpire’s signal is blocked by the non-striker. Connor Reed later bowls Arin, but a wide earlier in that over means the wall-clock sequence cannot be used as the legal-ball count. The television wicket strip includes the earlier duplicate from the Carter stand and is therefore a provisional score state.

The delivery authority resolves the Carter-Arin duplication by rejecting the automatic packet and preserving the live wide call. That single event decision propagates through the team stream, the partnership extras channel and Arin’s personal attribution cache; no terminal message states any of their final values. Evan’s seven remains untouched. A stand snapshot from before the decision continues circulating in a replay package. The authoritative second-wicket state, the event components and the rejected packet together are required to recover the completed Carter-Arin association rather than choosing between the radio and television cards by recency.

A side-on replay later settles Tyler’s sweep as leg byes. The authority references the Arin partnership delivery, not the superficially similar first-innings pad events. Tyler’s provisional share changes ledger, while the team and partnership values do not. After Arin’s dismissal, Tyler adds seven with Aiden Scott before Dylan Vale catches him from Aaron Miles. The archive then replays the sweep beside Tyler’s catch, but one is a scoring-attribution event and the other a dismissal. Their shared batter must not merge them. Tyler takes no part in another partnership after the catch.

Connor’s over record supplies the legal-ball detail for Arin’s dismissal: eleven overs were complete, a wide interrupted the sequence, and the wicket delivery is the fourth legitimate ball thereafter. The preceding wicket state is Evan’s authoritative boundary, and the Tyler-Arin event stream supplies the intervening score movement. The provisional post-wicket strip is one unit too high because of the Carter-stand packet that has since been rejected. The official terminal accepts Connor as bowler and Arin as the third dismissed batter without publishing a formatted fall-of-wicket line.

Blake Morgan is bowled by Aaron Miles after Tyler’s catch. A big-screen replay of Tyler’s dismissal follows immediately, and an automated highlight counter briefly groups both clips as fresh Aaron events. Their delivery signatures separate the new Blake wicket from the old Tyler view. Julian Vale is then bowled by Connor Reed, and Aiden Scott is caught from Tyler Quinn’s bowling. These intervening dismissals matter because the late Aaron sequence is not continuous. A montage sorted by bowler surname is useful evidence only after every batter, over phase and dismissal mode has been resolved.

The chase-wide ledger continues to arrive in fragments. Connor’s spell contains two accepted wides and Aaron’s contains two. Tyler’s later spell has one. A legal dot following a graphics reconnect is nevertheless entered as a wide on the television ribbon because the automatic parser sees the bowler reset his mark. The delivery authority has the ball recorded as valid and scoreless, with no umpire signal. It places that packet in quarantine. The team strip and a stand-extras panel retain the television version, while the bowling cards do not support it.

Leo Foster survives several overs before Aaron Miles bowls him. Slow motion from behind the arm is stored as another clip with the same batter, bowler and delivery position. The highlight counter provisionally treats the view as an additional wicket. Cameron Ellis later advances to Aaron’s flighted ball and is stumped by Owen Hayes. The batting and partnership terminals accept Cameron’s departure immediately, yet a bowling-cache interruption means Aaron’s personal panel does not receive that event at first. Thus one authentic dismissal is absent while one replay duplicate is present, producing a plausible but structurally wrong local ledger.

Aiden’s dismissal and Leo’s fall define a later chase boundary. Between them, the official team record moves through a small Leo-Cameron partnership whose extras include legitimate wides. The director repeatedly uses the same Leo slow motion while commentators discuss Aaron’s control. The registry matches that view to the live delivery by batter, bowler and over position, then retires the replay packet. Aaron’s cache still lacks a different late event, so the locally displayed wicket state remains plausible but unclosed.

The delivery authority now rejects the television’s legal-dot wide. It identifies the packet by ball signature and the absence of an umpire signal, without displaying the revised chase-wide category. Caleb, Finn, Logan, Connor, Aaron and Tyler have already supplied their accepted spell components on separate graphics. The chase also contains no byes, one no-ball from Connor, and pad-contact units whose accepted leg-bye record consists of three events. Those categories can be reconciled against the team ledger, but no single card presents their aggregate.

At the scorer’s desk, Arin’s stale player profile and Aaron’s interrupted bowling cache arrive in the same archive batch. The profile predates the Carter-window packet decision, while the authoritative attribution ledger is versioned after Evan’s wicket review. Neither screen repeats Arin’s other partnership components. On a separate rules channel, Cameron’s already accepted stumping signature is propagated into the bowler-credit cache because the delivery was legal and Aaron was the bowler. The message repairs event ownership without displaying either player’s completed row.

Dylan’s archive row receives a similar audit. His four with Finn is closed by Finn’s catch, his Connor component begins from the live fourteen but carries the separate packet ruling, his Evan component begins from ten but crosses the reviewed wicket boundary, and his Noah contribution is the settled thirty-seven. The two rulings concern different deliveries and different ledger families, so neither can be applied twice. No graphic combines the four accepted components. The result must also remain compatible with the first-innings batter aggregate and the distant partnership boundaries.

Finn’s audit reaches across the opening, Rory, Carter and Dylan windows. The opening live component carries the pad decision, Rory’s scoreless stay contributes nothing, and the Carter window carries the boundary-camera decision. Finn records no scoring event after Carter’s dismissal before his own wicket; Dylan’s four and the two extras account for that short stand. The old wagon wheel and provisional Carter card remain tempting because each is individually coherent. Only the official delivery identities, plus the first-innings conservation ledger, determine which versions survive together.

The chase closes with Miles Benton bowled by Tyler Quinn after Zane Cooper has joined him. The legal-ball archive records twenty-four full overs and four further valid deliveries. The nine non-target Meridian batters together contribute twenty-one. The accepted extras families comprise the six dispersed bowler-wide components, the three pad-contact leg-bye events, Connor’s no-ball and no byes. Arin and Tyler supply the two target batting components. These separate ledgers reconcile to the terminal’s final state, although neither commentary team reads that state aloud and the television ribbon is removed before the handshake.

For the first innings, the archive’s third-wicket composite is also recoverable without a direct caption. Rory’s wicket fixes the lower score boundary. Finn and Carter’s accepted components and the five partnership extras determine the movement before Carter is caught. The dismissal occurs after twenty-three completed overs on the fourth valid ball of the next over; an earlier wide in the spell does not advance that legal count. The cached component cards predate the boundary ruling, so they cannot be copied into the fall-of-wicket string without version control.

For the chase’s third wicket, Evan’s accepted boundary is the lower state. The Tyler-Arin association consists of Arin’s settled ten, Tyler’s attribution after the pad ruling, and two extras. Connor’s wide in the dismissal over does not consume a legal delivery, and Arin’s bowled event is the fourth valid ball after eleven completed overs. The television wicket strip still carries the rejected Carter packet. The terminal history, not that newest-looking picture, governs both the score component and over notation.

The closing archive sweep links the two innings without mixing them. First-innings pad and wide decisions update Shoreline’s batting, extras and partnership ledgers; chase decisions update Arin, Tyler, the Carter association and Meridian’s extras. Zane’s and Benton’s wickets belong only to Shoreline’s innings, while Aaron’s events belong only to the chase. Every replay remains searchable, so recency alone is useless. The accepted graph is the set of delivery signatures endorsed by the official terminal, checked against batter conservation, extras conservation, partnership boundaries, wicket uniqueness and legal-ball state.

The engineering review treats the Shoreline innings as two synchronized streams rather than a sequence of independent card rows. The first stream begins with Finn's opening pad contact and continues through the Carter boundary. The second begins with Dylan's duplicated running packet and continues through the wide reconnect and the Benton-Zane ownership split. Either stream can be patched locally; the combined innings cannot accept both local patches.

The opening pad contact is visible on the striker camera, so the television branch assigns it to Finn. The umpire branch links the same delivery signature to the leg-bye signal. Because the team score advances under either interpretation, the disagreement survives the opening partnership and Rory's scoreless stay. It becomes consequential only when Finn's cross-partnership batter components, the Finn-Carter boundary and the innings extras classes are conserved together.

The Carter stand contains a second packet that the boundary camera places after Carter's dismissal signature. A venue branch keeps it within the stand because the pictures are contiguous; the event branch attaches it to the following association. Each branch can produce a coherent local partnership ribbon by choosing the matching upper boundary. Only the independently sealed third-wicket state and the delivery transition decide which boundary is permitted.

Dylan's running event creates the same kind of coupled ambiguity. The automatic packet and the live scoring record share a running signature. Keeping both shifts Dylan's innings line and the downstream team states; collapsing the mirror changes the Connor and Evan windows used to reconstruct him. The reconnect wide packet and the accepted bowler-wide cards supply a separate conservation channel, so a compensating edit to Dylan alone does not close the innings.

Bowling ownership is deliberately not summarized. A surname-only Miles caption can refer to Carter the batter, Benton the bowler or Aaron in the later chase. The registry attaches credits only when a live delivery signature, dismissed batter and incoming-batter transition agree. Alternate camera angles for the Zane and Benton dismissals remain mirror nodes. This partition is checked against ten distinct first-innings dismissals rather than a television wicket numeral.

In the chase, the Carter-Arin feed opens one live wide and one automatic packet. A player-profile branch consumes both and lowers the remaining extras needed elsewhere; the authority branch merges the packet with the live call. Tyler's later pad event then determines whether a unit stays with his bat or enters a non-batter channel. Both choices can be made to fit a short local partnership graphic, but they cannot both satisfy Arin's cross-window account, Tyler's later contribution, the accepted chase-wide signatures and the third-wicket boundary.

Aaron's bowling cache is part of that same component. Tyler and Blake have distinct live dismissal signatures, Leo's slow motion is a mirror of his live ball, and Cameron's stumping propagates a bowler credit from a legal delivery. A cache that counts the mirror but misses the stumping reaches a plausible local total. It fails the owner registry even though the numeral happens to balance. The review therefore closes event edges, not bowler rows.

The terminal register supplies no completed scorecard. For Shoreline it preserves the legal closing position, the third-wicket event boundary, the accepted extras categories and a one-owner rule for every fallen batter. An admissible state must use one edge for each live scoring or dismissal event, may use mirror clips only as evidence, and must conserve batter and extras streams against the terminal state. Dropping any one rule leaves both engineering patches feasible.

For Meridian the register preserves the first- and second-wicket boundaries, the fourth legitimate ball of Connor's over for the third wicket, the terminal legal-ball position and the accepted source hierarchy. It requires the Carter-Arin packet, Tyler pad attribution and Aaron stumping propagation to be solved together. The player profile, television ribbon and bowling cache are provisional views; the delivery authority and terminal registry control the surviving graph.

documents.text:
The archive opens on a blustery afternoon at South Meridian Institute Ground, where Shoreline Rangers bat first and the production truck is running three score feeds at once. The television ribbon follows a wireless scorer, the radio booth keeps a handwritten sheet, and the official terminal accepts only messages carrying a delivery signature. Finn Archer begins fluently while Leo Marsh plays himself in. During the opening exchange, a glance is keyed to Finn by the television operator, although the umpire is screened by the striker. That key survives on the wagon-wheel graphic. The radio caller notes that the signal is obscured and declines to settle whether the contact was bat or pad.

Leo starts finding gaps after the first drinks runner has left the field. Two completed byes are visible in the keeper’s notebook, while three wides are scattered across Tyler Quinn’s opening spell. Finn’s share of the stand appears as forty on the live ribbon; Leo’s settled share is eighteen. A separate stand card contains five extras, but it is time-stamped before the contact query is examined. The team state at Leo’s dismissal is recorded by the official terminal as sixty-two for the first wicket. Aiden Scott takes the catch from Zane Cooper, and both radio and television attach the same delivery signature to that departure.

The replay director shows Leo’s catch twice, once from long-on and once from behind the bowler. The image classifier opens two clips, yet the official event record has the same striker, bowler, over position and wicket state on each. Rory Blake then blocks one ball and is bowled by Zane on the next without the score moving. His dismissal is a different signature, despite using the same bowler and appearing in the same montage. The radio sheet has Zane associated with both batters. A cached television counter briefly treats the second view of Leo’s catch as another wicket and carries that mistake into the next graphic.

Miles Carter joins Finn after Rory’s scoreless visit. The score boundary remains the state recorded after Leo because nothing came from Rory’s two balls. Finn drives through cover, Miles works the leg side, and five runs not credited to either batter are retained on the partnership strip. A provisional component card gives Finn thirty-six and Miles thirty-seven. It is not a completed partnership record: the boundary camera has marked a running event near the later dismissal for inspection, and neither card says on which side of the wicket that event belongs. The television total remains plausible, since moving the event across the boundary would not alter the innings aggregate.

The same delivery package later appears in a highlights queue under the label “Miles caught.” That caption refers to Miles Carter, the batter, rather than Miles Benton, the bowler who will appear elsewhere in the innings. Julian Vale is the catcher and Aiden Scott delivered the ball. The official terminal closes Carter’s batting event with those three identities. Its partnership message references the boundary marker but does not publish either batter’s revised share. Finn continues with Dylan Vale, who makes four during their brief overlap. The stand ends when Arin Wells catches Finn from Benton; two extras crossed during that short association.

At the start of Dylan’s next partnership, Connor Wells settles into defence while the television cache keeps Finn’s old contribution tile in a corner. Dylan is provisionally assigned fourteen during this association. A low side-on view of one hurried single is held for the umpire liaison because the ball may have brushed the pad. Connor’s eventual dismissal comes from Zane, who beats him with a straight ball. A lower-third retained from Zane’s spell also contains two accepted wides, without an innings-wide aggregate. The wicket’s batter identity, partnership boundary and over phase distinguish it from Rory’s similar-looking event.

The scoring liaison now resolves the opening glance. Rather than publishing a batter tally, the liaison sends the original delivery signature with the umpire’s leg-bye signal. The official terminal transfers that scoring unit from Finn’s personal event to the extras family while preserving the opening stand and team states. The old wagon wheel remains available as an archive image and still shows the live operator’s allocation. A second contact query from later in the innings is reviewed at the same time, but the signature belongs to Dylan and Connor, not Finn and Leo. The archive therefore contains similar-looking disputes whose records resolve through different scoring rules.

Dylan’s reviewed single reaches the archive as a live scoring record and an automatic packet carrying the same running signature. The side-on frame does not yet settle whether the visible contact should govern either packet. The terminal marks the records as linked and sends them to a later authority queue. Connor’s own twelve is already closed on the radio sheet, and one cached partnership strip still shows Dylan’s provisional figure. Both a bat-event version and a pad-event version remain locally plausible until the source hierarchy and wicket boundary are revisited.

Evan Price follows Connor. Dylan’s contribution in that passage first appears as ten, while Evan’s settled contribution is six. At Evan’s dismissal, Aiden Scott is the bowler and the ball hits the stumps. A transition packet containing the final running event reaches television before the official scorer attaches the wicket boundary. Noah Grant is already approaching in the wide shot. A fielding-spell recap elsewhere shows Blake Morgan with no wides and Evan Carter with two accepted calls; neither belongs to this batting transition. The archive desk flags the running packet without declaring which association will retain it.

Noah and Dylan produce the longest late recovery. Dylan’s accepted contribution in this association is thirty-seven and Noah’s is twenty-four, with seven extras appearing in the stand event stream. Miles Benton has Dylan caught by Isaac Vale. The television cuts immediately to Finn’s earlier catch, then to Noah’s later dismissal, so three Benton events sit together even though they occurred in separate partnerships. Each carries a distinct batter and delivery signature. The radio book also has Aaron Miles bowled by Benton between Dylan and Noah, while the producer’s montage initially omits that shorter event because it lacks a catch image.

An official boundary message eventually attaches the disputed transition run to Noah’s association. The message identifies Evan’s dismissal as the boundary and references the running event, but it does not quote Dylan’s completed innings figure. The cached strip is retained for broadcast chronology. At roughly the same time, a second camera angle of Dylan’s catch is ingested as a fresh clip; the archive registry links it to the existing Benton event. A separate spell graphic assigns Benton three accepted wides, information that has no authority over the duplicate camera view.

Aaron Miles is bowled by Benton in the lower order, and Noah is later caught from Benton with Arin Wells completing the chance. Their signatures enter the registry at different partnership states and are not summarized with earlier credits. The surname-only Carter caption is held outside the ledger pending role resolution, while Logan Shaw’s final bowled event carries Cameron Ellis’s delivery identifier. The radio booth places several Miles surnames on one hurried page, making that page unsafe without event ownership. The terminal accepts or rejects individual signatures but withholds Benton’s closed bowling panel.

The first-innings wides channel is meanwhile noisy. During Aiden Scott’s spell, the radio book contains three umpire-called wides. A graphics reconnect then emits another packet with the same ball signature, unchanged striker state and no fresh signal. The television ribbon accepts both and rises to a locally plausible state; the wireless scorer marks the pair for comparison but does not yet declare which record survives. Other bowlers’ components are absent from this screen, so neither the ribbon nor the radio page can close the innings-wide category here.

During the final overs Toby Reed counterattacks, Logan Shaw is bowled by Cameron, and the last legal-ball state is preserved as forty-seven completed overs plus two further valid deliveries. Cameron’s spell graphic carries four accepted wides, while the unresolved refresh remains on another feed. A delayed liaison message now confirms bat on Dylan’s Connor single; the delivery registry preserves the live record and rejects its automatic copy. The official batting ledger gives the nine non-target Shoreline batters one hundred twenty-four, with two byes and a no-ball settled separately, but no completed innings state is read aloud.

At the innings break the boundary camera’s decision on the Finn-Carter stand is released. The running event occurred after Carter’s dismissal signature had closed the partnership, so it belongs to the next association. The official terminal rejects that event from both provisional batter components attached to the completed stand. Finn’s and Carter’s accepted shares require the event identity and remote score boundaries. On a different console, the wireless scorer preserves Aiden’s original wide signature and retires the reconnect copy. Neither decision publishes a completed stand or innings-wide total.

The innings-review editor now tests whether every fallen-batter record has one owner. Alternate camera angles are joined to their original delivery signatures before any bowler partition is closed. A surname-only “Miles” caption remains quarantined until batter, bowler and catcher roles are recovered from the live call. The editor checks the accepted registry against the ten distinct departures, but the review screen displays neither Zane’s nor Benton’s completed column. That global partition can expose an omitted or repeated event without supplying a local numerical verdict.

Meridian Strikers begin the chase with Arin Wells taking the only scoring run before Isaac Vale is leg before to Caleb Turner. The official terminal closes that first-wicket state at the fourth legal ball. Two preview clips use the same signature, so only the live event enters Caleb’s ledger. Evan Carter joins Arin. The radio sheet gives Evan seven for their partnership, while the live stand-extras box opens at seven. Arin’s component is hidden by a weather banner. The feed remains provisional because one of those extras came from an automatic scoring packet that may duplicate an umpire call.

Caleb’s full spell contains six accepted wides, spread across several overs rather than concentrated around Isaac’s dismissal. Finn Archer later bowls a short spell with one, and Logan Shaw’s spell contains none. These bowling figures appear during interviews and are not adjacent to the chase extras panel. In the Carter-Arin stand, the suspicious packet has the same delivery identifier, striker and non-striker state as a wide already called live. The official scorer quarantines it, but the television stand card continues to carry both entries. Team, partnership and Arin’s cached attribution all remain locally plausible until the authoritative packet decision arrives.

Evan is bowled by Logan Shaw. The official wicket event is accepted at the second legal delivery after six completed overs, and the previous first-wicket state remains in terminal history. The television ribbon momentarily shows the chase at twenty-eight for two because it carries the duplicate packet. A cached player tile, issued from that same feed, assigns Arin fourteen within the Carter window. The radio caller has a lower team state but cannot explain the difference live. The terminal references the suspect signature in a correction queue rather than printing either a settled partnership or personal total.

Tyler and Arin rotate strike through a cautious passage. Arin’s accepted contribution during this association is ten, while two extras are tied to legal-ball and wide records elsewhere. Tyler’s provisional personal tile says seven. One sweep hits pad before travelling into the outfield; the umpire’s signal is blocked by the non-striker. Connor Reed later bowls Arin, but a wide earlier in that over means the wall-clock sequence cannot be used as the legal-ball count. The television wicket strip includes the earlier duplicate from the Carter stand and is therefore a provisional score state.

The delivery authority resolves the Carter-Arin duplication by rejecting the automatic packet and preserving the live wide call. That single event decision propagates through the team stream, the partnership extras channel and Arin’s personal attribution cache; no terminal message states any of their final values. Evan’s seven remains untouched. A stand snapshot from before the decision continues circulating in a replay package. The authoritative second-wicket state, the event components and the rejected packet together are required to recover the completed Carter-Arin association rather than choosing between the radio and television cards by recency.

A side-on replay later settles Tyler’s sweep as leg byes. The authority references the Arin partnership delivery, not the superficially similar first-innings pad events. Tyler’s provisional share changes ledger, while the team and partnership values do not. After Arin’s dismissal, Tyler adds seven with Aiden Scott before Dylan Vale catches him from Aaron Miles. The archive then replays the sweep beside Tyler’s catch, but one is a scoring-attribution event and the other a dismissal. Their shared batter must not merge them. Tyler takes no part in another partnership after the catch.

Connor’s over record supplies the legal-ball detail for Arin’s dismissal: eleven overs were complete, a wide interrupted the sequence, and the wicket delivery is the fourth legitimate ball thereafter. The preceding wicket state is Evan’s authoritative boundary, and the Tyler-Arin event stream supplies the intervening score movement. The provisional post-wicket strip is one unit too high because of the Carter-stand packet that has since been rejected. The official terminal accepts Connor as bowler and Arin as the third dismissed batter without publishing a formatted fall-of-wicket line.

Blake Morgan is bowled by Aaron Miles after Tyler’s catch. A big-screen replay of Tyler’s dismissal follows immediately, and an automated highlight counter briefly groups both clips as fresh Aaron events. Their delivery signatures separate the new Blake wicket from the old Tyler view. Julian Vale is then bowled by Connor Reed, and Aiden Scott is caught from Tyler Quinn’s bowling. These intervening dismissals matter because the late Aaron sequence is not continuous. A montage sorted by bowler surname is useful evidence only after every batter, over phase and dismissal mode has been resolved.

The chase-wide ledger continues to arrive in fragments. Connor’s spell contains two accepted wides and Aaron’s contains two. Tyler’s later spell has one. A legal dot following a graphics reconnect is nevertheless entered as a wide on the television ribbon because the automatic parser sees the bowler reset his mark. The delivery authority has the ball recorded as valid and scoreless, with no umpire signal. It places that packet in quarantine. The team strip and a stand-extras panel retain the television version, while the bowling cards do not support it.

Leo Foster survives several overs before Aaron Miles bowls him. Slow motion from behind the arm is stored as another clip with the same batter, bowler and delivery position. The highlight counter provisionally treats the view as an additional wicket. Cameron Ellis later advances to Aaron’s flighted ball and is stumped by Owen Hayes. The batting and partnership terminals accept Cameron’s departure immediately, yet a bowling-cache interruption means Aaron’s personal panel does not receive that event at first. Thus one authentic dismissal is absent while one replay duplicate is present, producing a plausible but structurally wrong local ledger.

Aiden’s dismissal and Leo’s fall define a later chase boundary. Between them, the official team record moves through a small Leo-Cameron partnership whose extras include legitimate wides. The director repeatedly uses the same Leo slow motion while commentators discuss Aaron’s control. The registry matches that view to the live delivery by batter, bowler and over position, then retires the replay packet. Aaron’s cache still lacks a different late event, so the locally displayed wicket state remains plausible but unclosed.

The delivery authority now rejects the television’s legal-dot wide. It identifies the packet by ball signature and the absence of an umpire signal, without displaying the revised chase-wide category. Caleb, Finn, Logan, Connor, Aaron and Tyler have already supplied their accepted spell components on separate graphics. The chase also contains no byes, one no-ball from Connor, and pad-contact units whose accepted leg-bye record consists of three events. Those categories can be reconciled against the team ledger, but no single card presents their aggregate.

At the scorer’s desk, Arin’s stale player profile and Aaron’s interrupted bowling cache arrive in the same archive batch. The profile predates the Carter-window packet decision, while the authoritative attribution ledger is versioned after Evan’s wicket review. Neither screen repeats Arin’s other partnership components. On a separate rules channel, Cameron’s already accepted stumping signature is propagated into the bowler-credit cache because the delivery was legal and Aaron was the bowler. The message repairs event ownership without displaying either player’s completed row.

Dylan’s archive row receives a similar audit. His four with Finn is closed by Finn’s catch, his Connor component begins from the live fourteen but carries the separate packet ruling, his Evan component begins from ten but crosses the reviewed wicket boundary, and his Noah contribution is the settled thirty-seven. The two rulings concern different deliveries and different ledger families, so neither can be applied twice. No graphic combines the four accepted components.
